description: Defining classes with properties, methods, events and enumerations, the difference between value and handle semantics, class introspection, and the functions that manipulate MATLAB's built-in container types: structures, cell arrays, maps and dictionaries.

tools.name: classdef
tools.description: Begins a class definition file, optionally listing superclasses and class attributes such as Abstract, Sealed and ConstructOnLoad. The file name must match the class name, and the body contains properties, methods, events and enumeration blocks. Use classes to bundle data with the operations on it and to enforce invariants through property validation.
tools.usage:
classdef ClassName
    ...
end
classdef ClassName < SuperClass
classdef (Abstract) ClassName
classdef ClassName < handle & matlab.mixin.Copyable

parameters.name: < SuperClass
parameters.description: Base class or classes, combined with &.

parameters.name: (Abstract)
parameters.description: Class cannot be instantiated directly.

parameters.name: (Sealed)
parameters.description: Class cannot be subclassed.

parameters.name: (ConstructOnLoad)
parameters.description: Call the constructor when loading from a MAT-file.

tools.example:
classdef Sensor
    properties
        Name (1,1) string = "unnamed"
        Gain (1,1) double {mustBePositive} = 1
    end
    methods
        function obj = Sensor(name, gain)
            if nargin > 0
                obj.Name = name;
                obj.Gain = gain;
            end
        end
        function y = apply(obj, x)
            y = obj.Gain * x;
        end
    end
end

% s = Sensor("probe", 2.5); s.apply(4)
tools.notes: A class in a file must be the only classdef in that file, and the file must be on the path. Classes can also live in a package folder named +pkg, in which case they are referred to as pkg.ClassName.

tools.name: properties
tools.description: Declares a block of class properties with optional size, class and validator specifications, default values and attributes such as Access, Dependent, Constant and SetObservable. As a function, `properties(obj)` lists the public property names of an object or class. Use property validation to enforce invariants automatically on every assignment.
tools.usage:
properties
    Name (1,1) string = ""
end
properties (Access = private)
properties (Constant)
properties (Dependent)
p = properties(obj)

parameters.name: Access
parameters.description: 'public' (default), 'private', 'protected', or a list of classes.

parameters.name: Constant
parameters.description: Value fixed at class definition time and shared by all instances.

parameters.name: Dependent
parameters.description: Computed on access by a get method rather than stored.

parameters.name: SetObservable/GetObservable
parameters.description: Allow listeners on property access (handle classes only).

parameters.name: Transient
parameters.description: Not saved when the object is serialized.

tools.example:
classdef Circle
    properties
        Radius (1,1) double {mustBePositive} = 1
    end
    properties (Dependent)
        Area
    end
    properties (Constant)
        Units = "m"
    end
    methods
        function a = get.Area(obj)
            a = pi * obj.Radius^2;
        end
    end
end

% c = Circle; c.Radius = 2; c.Area
% properties(Circle)
tools.notes: Property validation runs on every assignment, including inside the class, which makes invalid states impossible but costs a little performance in hot loops. Dependent properties are not stored, so they never go stale.

tools.name: methods
tools.description: Declares a block of class methods with shared attributes such as Access, Static, Abstract and Hidden. As a function, `methods(obj)` lists the callable methods of a class. Ordinary methods take the object as their first argument, while Static methods do not and are called with the class name.
tools.usage:
methods
    function out = f(obj, x)
    end
end
methods (Static)
methods (Access = protected)
methods (Abstract)
m = methods(obj)
m = methods(obj, '-full')

parameters.name: Access
parameters.description: Visibility of the methods in the block.

parameters.name: Static
parameters.description: Methods called on the class rather than an instance.

parameters.name: Abstract
parameters.description: Signature only; subclasses must implement it.

parameters.name: Sealed
parameters.description: Cannot be overridden by subclasses.

tools.example:
classdef Converter
    methods (Static)
        function c = f2c(f)
            c = (f - 32) * 5/9;
        end
    end
    methods
        function show(obj)
            disp(class(obj));
        end
    end
end

% Converter.f2c(212)
% methods(Converter)
tools.notes: Calling a method as `obj.method(args)` and as `method(obj, args)` are equivalent for non-static methods. A constructor is a method with the same name as the class that returns the object.

tools.name: events
tools.description: Declares named events that a handle class can broadcast, allowing other code to react without the class knowing about its listeners. Trigger an event with `notify` and subscribe with `addlistener`. Use events for loosely coupled designs such as apps, simulations and data pipelines.
tools.usage:
events
    EventName
end
events (ListenAccess = public, NotifyAccess = private)
notify(obj, 'EventName')
notify(obj, 'EventName', eventData)

parameters.name: ListenAccess
parameters.description: Who may listen: 'public' (default), 'protected', 'private'.

parameters.name: NotifyAccess
parameters.description: Who may trigger the event.

tools.example:
classdef Counter < handle
    properties
        Value = 0
    end
    events
        LimitReached
    end
    methods
        function increment(obj)
            obj.Value = obj.Value + 1;
            if obj.Value >= 3
                notify(obj, 'LimitReached');
            end
        end
    end
end

% c = Counter;
% addlistener(c, 'LimitReached', @(src, evt) disp('limit!'));
% for k = 1:3, c.increment(); end
tools.notes: Only handle classes can define events, because value classes are copied on assignment and listeners would attach to the wrong copy. Custom event data requires subclassing `event.EventData`.

tools.name: enumeration
tools.description: Declares a fixed set of named instances of a class, giving MATLAB a type-safe alternative to magic strings and numbers. Enumeration members can carry constructor arguments so each name maps to a value. As a function, `enumeration(ClassName)` lists the members.
tools.usage:
classdef Color
    enumeration
        Red, Green, Blue
    end
end
enumeration(ClassName)
[members, names] = enumeration(ClassName)

parameters.name: member names
parameters.description: Names of the enumeration members, with optional constructor arguments in parentheses.

tools.example:
classdef Weekday < double
    enumeration
        Monday (1)
        Tuesday (2)
        Wednesday (3)
    end
end

% d = Weekday.Tuesday;
% double(d)
% d == Weekday.Tuesday
% enumeration(Weekday)
tools.notes: Deriving the enumeration from a built-in type such as double or int32 lets members be used directly in arithmetic and comparisons. Enumerations work well in `switch` statements and in `mustBeMember` validation.

tools.name: handle
tools.description: The base class that gives reference semantics: variables referring to a handle object all point to the same underlying data, so modifying it through one variable is visible through all of them. Value classes, the default, copy on assignment instead. Use handle classes for objects with identity such as GUI components, simulation entities and shared resources.
tools.usage:
classdef MyClass < handle
    ...
end
delete(obj)
tf = isvalid(obj)
b = eq(obj1, obj2)
tools.example:
classdef Node < handle
    properties
        Value = 0
    end
end

% a = Node; b = a;
% b.Value = 5;
% a.Value        % 5, because a and b are the same object
%
% Value class contrast:
% s.Value = 0; t = s; t.Value = 5; s.Value   % still 0
tools.notes: Handle objects are not automatically copied, so functions that modify them change the caller's object; that is the point, but it surprises people used to MATLAB's value semantics. Inherit from `matlab.mixin.Copyable` to get a `copy` method, and call `delete` to invalidate a handle explicitly.

tools.name: superclasses
tools.description: Lists the names of all superclasses of a class or object, showing the inheritance chain. Use it to understand unfamiliar class hierarchies and to verify that a class inherits from an expected mixin. It returns a cell array of character vectors.
tools.usage:
s = superclasses(ClassName)
s = superclasses(obj)

parameters.name: ClassName
parameters.description: Class name as text, or an object of that class.

tools.notes: It lists only visible superclasses; hidden ones are omitted. For programmatic checks, `isa(obj, 'ClassName')` is simpler and also covers built-in category names.

tools.name: metaclass
tools.description: Returns a meta.class object that describes a class in full: its properties, methods, events, attributes and superclasses, each with their own attributes. Use it for reflection, for generating documentation, and for writing frameworks that adapt to a class's structure. `?ClassName` is the shorthand syntax.
tools.usage:
mc = metaclass(obj)
mc = ?ClassName
mc.PropertyList
mc.MethodList

parameters.name: obj
parameters.description: Object whose class is described.

parameters.name: ?ClassName
parameters.description: Literal syntax giving the meta.class for a named class.

tools.notes: Comparing Access attributes requires care because Access can be a cell array of meta.class objects for restricted access, not just a string. meta.class objects are handle objects and reflect the class as currently defined.

tools.name: isprop
tools.description: Tests whether an object has a property with a given name, returning a logical value. Use it in generic code that must work with several object types, and to check optional properties before accessing them. It works on graphics objects as well as user-defined classes.
tools.usage: tf = isprop(obj, propName)

parameters.name: obj
parameters.description: Object or object array.

parameters.name: propName
parameters.description: Property name, or a cell/string array of names.

tools.example:
h = plot(1:10);
isprop(h, 'LineWidth')
isprop(h, 'FaceColor')
isprop(h, {'Color', 'Marker', 'Nope'})
if isprop(h, 'LineWidth'), h.LineWidth = 2; end
tools.notes: isprop returns false for private properties when called from outside the class. For structures use `isfield` instead, and for methods use `ismethod`.

tools.name: ismethod
tools.description: Tests whether a class defines a method with a given name. Use it in duck-typed code that calls a method only if the object supports it, and in framework code that dispatches on capability. It does not find functions that merely overload an operator for the class unless they are declared as methods.
tools.usage:
tf = ismethod(obj, methodName)
tf = ismethod(ClassName, methodName)

parameters.name: obj
parameters.description: Object or class name.

parameters.name: methodName
parameters.description: Method name to look for.

tools.notes: It reports methods visible from the calling context, so private methods return false from outside the class. Combine with `isprop` when writing code that must work across several unrelated object types.

tools.name: isobject
tools.description: Tests whether a value is an object of a user-defined or MathWorks class, as opposed to a built-in fundamental type such as double, char, cell or struct. Use it in generic code that must branch between plain data and objects. Note that many modern MATLAB types such as string, table and datetime are objects.
tools.usage: tf = isobject(A)

parameters.name: A
parameters.description: Any value.

tools.example:
isobject(1)
isobject('abc')
isobject(struct('a',1))
isobject(containers.Map)
isobject(table())
isobject(datetime('now'))
tools.notes: `isobject` is false for struct and cell even though they are containers. For a specific type test, `isa(x, 'ClassName')` is almost always the better choice.

tools.name: isvalid
tools.description: Tests whether handle objects are still valid, that is not yet deleted. Deleted handles remain as variables but cannot be used, so checking before access avoids errors. Use it in callbacks and long-lived code that holds references to figures, timers and other objects the user may have closed.
tools.usage: tf = isvalid(obj)

parameters.name: obj
parameters.description: Handle object or array of handle objects.

tools.notes: Only handle objects can be invalid; value objects are always valid. Callbacks that run after a window closes are a common source of 'Invalid or deleted object' errors, which an isvalid guard prevents.

tools.name: delete
tools.description: Deletes handle objects, invalidating every reference to them and releasing their resources, or deletes files from disk when given a file name. For handle classes you can define a `delete` method that runs as a destructor to release external resources. Use it to close figures, stop timers and clean up objects that hold file or hardware handles.
tools.usage:
delete(obj)
delete(filename)
delete('*.tmp')

parameters.name: obj
parameters.description: Handle object or array to destroy.

parameters.name: filename
parameters.description: File or wildcard pattern to delete from disk.

tools.notes: Whether `delete` removes files permanently or moves them to the recycle bin depends on the `recycle` setting, which defaults to off for the file form. Deleting a handle does not clear the variable, which remains as an invalid handle.

tools.name: addlistener
tools.description: Attaches a callback function to an event or to a property change on a handle object, returning a listener object whose lifetime controls the subscription. Use it to react to state changes without polling and to connect app components. Property listeners require the property to be declared SetObservable or GetObservable.
tools.usage:
lh = addlistener(obj, eventName, callback)
lh = addlistener(obj, propName, 'PostSet', callback)
lh = addlistener(obj, propName, 'PreSet', callback)
lh = listener(obj, eventName, callback)

parameters.name: eventName
parameters.description: Name of the event to listen for.

parameters.name: propName
parameters.description: Property name for property-change listeners.

parameters.name: 'PostSet'/'PreSet'/'PostGet'/'PreGet'
parameters.description: Which property access to observe.

parameters.name: callback
parameters.description: Function handle taking (source, eventData).

tools.notes: A listener created with `addlistener` is owned by the object and lives as long as it does; `listener` returns one whose lifetime you control, so it must be stored or it is removed immediately. Delete listeners explicitly to avoid callbacks firing on stale state.

tools.name: notify
tools.description: Broadcasts an event from a handle object, invoking every registered listener callback synchronously in an unspecified order. Optional event data derived from `event.EventData` carries extra information to the listeners. Use it inside class methods at the points where meaningful state changes occur.
tools.usage:
notify(obj, eventName)
notify(obj, eventName, eventData)

parameters.name: eventName
parameters.description: Name of an event declared in the class.

parameters.name: eventData
parameters.description: Object derived from event.EventData carrying extra information.

tools.notes: Listener callbacks run synchronously, so a slow listener blocks the notifying code. An error thrown in one listener prevents the remaining listeners from running.

tools.name: copy
tools.description: Creates an independent copy of a handle object whose class inherits from matlab.mixin.Copyable. By default it performs a shallow copy of property values; override copyElement to implement deep copying of nested handle properties. Use it when you need value-like duplication of an object that otherwise has reference semantics.

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Copyable handle object or array.

tools.example:
classdef Config < matlab.mixin.Copyable
    properties
        Gain = 1
    end
end

% a = Config; b = copy(a); b.Gain = 5;
% a.Gain     % still 1
% c = a; c.Gain = 9;
% a.Gain     % 9, because c is the same object
tools.notes: A shallow copy shares any handle objects stored in properties, so both copies see changes to them; override copyElement and call `copy` on those properties for a deep copy. Value classes do not need Copyable because assignment already copies.

tools.name: dictionary
tools.description: Creates a dictionary mapping unique keys to values, with support for string, numeric and other key types and fast lookup. Introduced in R2022b, it is recommended over containers.Map because it has value semantics, supports vectorized lookup and integrates with the rest of the language. Use it for lookup tables, counters and sparse associative data.
tools.usage:
d = dictionary(keys, values)
d = dictionary(k1, v1, ..., kN, vN)
d = configureDictionary(keyType, valueType)
v = d(key)
d(key) = value
k = keys(d)
v = values(d)

parameters.name: keys
parameters.description: Array of unique keys.

parameters.name: values
parameters.description: Corresponding values; a cell array allows heterogeneous values.

parameters.name: keyType, valueType
parameters.description: Class names for `configureDictionary`, for example "string" and "double".

tools.notes: Dictionaries have value semantics, so passing one to a function that modifies it does not affect the caller's copy, unlike containers.Map. Looking up a missing key errors; test with `isKey` or use `lookup` with a FallbackValue.

tools.name: containers.Map
tools.description: The older hash map class, mapping character vector or numeric keys to arbitrary values with handle (reference) semantics. Use it when maintaining code written before R2022b; for new code `dictionary` is faster and better integrated. Keys and values are retrieved as cell arrays.
tools.usage:
M = containers.Map
M = containers.Map(keySet, valueSet)
M = containers.Map('KeyType', kt, 'ValueType', vt)
v = M(key)
M(key) = v
k = keys(M)
isKey(M, key)
remove(M, key)

parameters.name: keySet
parameters.description: Cell array of keys, all of the same type.

parameters.name: valueSet
parameters.description: Cell array of values.

parameters.name: 'KeyType'
parameters.description: 'char' (default), 'double', 'single', or an integer class.

parameters.name: 'ValueType'
parameters.description: 'any' (default) or a specific class.

tools.notes: containers.Map is a handle object, so a function that modifies it changes the caller's map; this differs from `dictionary` and is a frequent source of bugs. Lookup of a missing key raises an error, so guard with `isKey`.

tools.name: fieldnames
tools.description: Returns the field names of a structure, or the public property names of an object, as a cell array of character vectors in definition order. Use it to iterate over all fields with dynamic field access and to compare the shape of two structures. For objects, `properties` is the preferred equivalent.
tools.usage:
names = fieldnames(S)
names = fieldnames(obj)
names = fieldnames(obj, '-full')

parameters.name: S
parameters.description: Structure array or object.

tools.notes: Dynamic field access `s.(name)` combined with fieldnames is the standard way to loop over a struct. Field order matters for `isequal` on structs only in that both must have the same set, not the same order.

tools.name: isfield
tools.description: Tests whether a structure contains fields with the given names, returning a logical array when several names are supplied. Use it to handle optional configuration fields and to validate structures received from elsewhere. It returns false for objects, where `isprop` is the right test.
tools.usage:
tf = isfield(S, field)
tf = isfield(S, fields)

parameters.name: S
parameters.description: Structure array.

parameters.name: field
parameters.description: Field name, or a cell/string array of names.

tools.example:
opts.gain = 2;
isfield(opts, 'gain')
isfield(opts, 'offset')
isfield(opts, {'gain','offset','mode'})
if ~isfield(opts, 'offset'), opts.offset = 0; end
tools.notes: isfield on a non-struct returns false rather than erroring, which makes it safe as a first guard. For nested structures you must test each level separately.

tools.name: rmfield
tools.description: Removes one or more fields from a structure, returning a new structure without them. Use it to strip large intermediate results before saving, and to drop fields that should not be exported. It errors if a named field does not exist.
tools.usage:
s = rmfield(s, field)
s = rmfield(s, fields)

parameters.name: s
parameters.description: Structure array.

parameters.name: field
parameters.description: Name or cell array of names to remove.

tools.notes: Removing a field that does not exist raises an error, so combine with `isfield` when the field is optional. rmfield returns a copy; it does not modify the original in place.

tools.name: setfield
tools.description: Sets the value of a field, including nested fields addressed by a chain of names and indices, and returns the modified structure. Dot notation is clearer for fixed names, so setfield is mainly useful when the path is computed at run time. It always returns the whole updated structure.
tools.usage:
s = setfield(s, field, value)
s = setfield(s, {i}, field, {j}, value)
s = setfield(s, path, value)

parameters.name: field
parameters.description: Field name, or a cell array describing a nested path with indices.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: New value.

tools.notes: Dynamic field syntax `s.(name) = value` does the same thing more readably for simple cases. setfield returns a new struct, so the assignment back to s is required.

tools.name: getfield
tools.description: Returns the value of a field, including nested paths with indices, from a structure. As with `setfield`, dynamic field syntax is preferable for simple cases and getfield shines when the path is data-driven. It errors when the field does not exist.
tools.usage:
value = getfield(s, field)
value = getfield(s, {i}, field, {j})

parameters.name: field
parameters.description: Field name or a nested path specification.

tools.notes: Chained dot access is faster and clearer; use getfield only for computed paths. Neither form creates missing fields, so check with `isfield` first.

tools.name: orderfields
tools.description: Reorders the fields of a structure alphabetically, to match another structure, or into an explicitly given order. Use it to normalize structures before comparison or display, and to produce consistent field ordering in saved files and JSON output. The data is unchanged; only the ordering differs.
tools.usage:
s = orderfields(s)
s = orderfields(s1, s2)
s = orderfields(s, cellOfNames)
s = orderfields(s, permutation)
[s, perm] = orderfields(___)

parameters.name: s2
parameters.description: Structure whose field order is copied.

parameters.name: cellOfNames
parameters.description: Explicit ordering of the field names.

parameters.name: permutation
parameters.description: Numeric permutation vector.

tools.notes: Ordering fields the same way in two structs makes `jsonencode` output and printed displays directly comparable. `isequal` on structs ignores field order already.

tools.name: struct2cell
tools.description: Converts a structure to a cell array containing the field values, with one page per element of a struct array. The field names are not included, so pair it with `fieldnames` to keep them. Use it to iterate over values generically and to feed struct data to functions expecting cell arrays.
tools.usage: C = struct2cell(S)

parameters.name: S
parameters.description: Structure array.

tools.notes: For a struct array the result is nfields-by-1-by-nelements, so `squeeze` is usually needed. `cell2struct` performs the reverse conversion and needs the field names supplied separately.

tools.name: cell2struct
tools.description: Builds a structure array from a cell array of values plus a list of field names, taking the fields along a specified dimension. Use it to turn parsed records into structures and to reverse a `struct2cell` conversion. The number of names must match the size along the chosen dimension.
tools.usage: S = cell2struct(C, fields, dim)

parameters.name: C
parameters.description: Cell array of values.

parameters.name: fields
parameters.description: Cell array or string array of field names.

parameters.name: dim
parameters.description: Dimension of C along which the fields lie.

tools.notes: Getting the dimension wrong produces a struct array of the wrong length rather than an error, so check `numel` of the result. Field names must be valid MATLAB identifiers.

tools.name: cell2mat
tools.description: Concatenates the contents of a cell array into a single array, respecting the cell array's own arrangement as a block layout. All cells must contain compatible types and matching dimensions along the joining directions. Use it to assemble results collected in a cell array inside a loop.
tools.usage: A = cell2mat(C)

parameters.name: C
parameters.description: Cell array whose contents concatenate into a rectangular array.

tools.notes: Collecting results in a cell array in a loop and calling cell2mat once at the end is much faster than concatenating into a growing array each iteration. `mat2cell` and `num2cell` perform the reverse conversions.

tools.name: num2cell
tools.description: Converts an array into a cell array with one element per array element, or per slice when dimensions are specified. Use it to produce a comma-separated list for functions that take several arguments, and to feed array data to cell-oriented functions. `deal` and `{:}` expansion are the usual companions.
tools.usage:
C = num2cell(A)
C = num2cell(A, dim)
C = num2cell(A, [dim1 dim2])

parameters.name: A
parameters.description: Array to split.

parameters.name: dim
parameters.description: Dimensions kept together inside each cell.

tools.notes: num2cell on a large array creates a cell per element, which uses far more memory than the array itself. `mat2cell` splits into blocks of chosen sizes instead.

tools.name: mat2cell
tools.description: Splits an array into a cell array of submatrices with sizes you specify for each dimension. The size vectors must sum to the corresponding array dimensions. Use it to divide data into blocks for block-wise processing, to split a signal into segments, and to partition a matrix by group sizes.
tools.usage:
C = mat2cell(A, dim1Dist)
C = mat2cell(A, dim1Dist, dim2Dist, ...)

parameters.name: dim1Dist
parameters.description: Vector of row counts for each block; must sum to size(A,1).

parameters.name: dim2Dist
parameters.description: Vector of column counts; must sum to size(A,2).

tools.notes: The distribution vectors must sum exactly to the array dimensions, otherwise mat2cell errors. Combine with `cellfun` to apply a function to each block.

tools.name: iscellstr
tools.description: Tests whether a value is a cell array in which every element is a character vector. Use it to validate inputs that must be a cell array of names, and to distinguish cellstr from string arrays and mixed cell arrays. It returns false for cell arrays containing strings or numbers.
tools.usage: tf = iscellstr(A)

parameters.name: A
parameters.description: Any value.

tools.example:
iscellstr({'a','bb','ccc'})
iscellstr({'a', 1})
iscellstr({"a", "b"})
iscellstr(["a" "b"])
isstring(["a" "b"])
tools.notes: A cell array of string scalars is not a cellstr, which trips up validation written before string arrays existed. `convertCharsToStrings` and `convertStringsToChars` help functions accept both conventions.
